quote: Maybe herein lies the perfect word to describe Terrifier 3. It separates. Skin from muscle. A lower jaw from the upper jaw. Left butt cheek from right butt cheek. Every way in which a body can be torn asunder, Terrifier 3 will separate.

Damien Leone ratcheted up the carnage as we follow the surviving siblings trying to move forward after the last film’s events when Art returns for more terror during the holidays. It’s a bloody all-you-can-eat feast for the eyes.
If the earlier films weren’t really your thing, this one probably won’t be either. But either way, Art the Clown is back with a vengeance, and Christmas just got a little more bloody.
Gleefully deranged and drenched in gore, Terrifier 3 gives Terrifier fans exactly what they want from the franchise and more to boot.

There can be a line ... between a good scarefest, offering suspense and the occasional jolt, and torture porn, in which the intended appeal appears to be the sadistic display of relentless brutality. Terrifier 3 gleefully crosses that line.
Damien Leone knows his audience and understands what it is they want out of a Terrifier story.
Leone smoothly transitions from a focus on folklore to a focus on religion, done almost as if to present the human struggle to have characters forgive themselves for their past misfortunes.
As an indie horror film, Terrifier 3 absolutely slays—pun intended.

A slight step down from the previous entry, Terrifier 3's split narrative often feels like two very different films forced into one with tonal shifts that lack finesse. Thornton and LaVera's performances elevate the wobbly execution, though.

The biggest drawback in Terrifier 3 is its role as a transitional chapter leading to an inevitable fourth installment which, if it continues along the current trend, could become a slasher cathedral remembered by future generations of fans.

While 2 remains the benchmark to beat, Terrifier 3 proves there's plenty of life left in David Howard Thorton's Art the Clown and the Christmas debauchery is extremely, extremely welcome (particularly the chainsaw scene)
The Terrifiers are anti-arthouse horror films that deliberately have nothing to say beyond gee aren’t we nasty? If you need me, I’ll be somewhere on the spectrum between ambivalent and bored.
Wonderfully gross, disturbing, dark and hilarious for any fan of slasher movies.
Terrifier 3 does not disappoint. It is bloody and bold and bloody and silly and bloody – did I mention it was bloody?

If you can imagine, it’s even more depraved, sadistic and just plain wrong. No one is spared: families, kids, lovers – all at the hands of a silent creature that finds absolute joy in others’ pain – and now in a Santa suit most of the time.

What last time around felt like a fresh, full-blooded geek show that was very much a love-letter to the slasher films of the 1970s and ‘80s instead reeks of recycled ideas, barely hanging together as a series of set-pieces.

Fans of the previous 2 Terrifier movies should know what to expect from this new installment. More gore, more thrills, more Art the Clown. What they might not be expecting is just how funny this one is. Art brings just as many laughs as he does carnage.
Terrifier 3’s success comes from never trying to be anything it is not. It is gross and it is engaging, and it refuses to apologize for being both
Part of the ultra-gory killer-clown horror series, the folks behind this Christmastime-set tale clearly put some thought and care into its characters, situations, and especially its bloody effects.

Leone’s devilish glee at getting away with what he’s getting away with—that all of this has somehow become successful—is legitimately infectious; this is easily the most accomplished film in the series, and it’s not just the bigger budget.

The most-metal Christmas horror movie ever made.

A reminder that the second Terrifier was more than just a commitment to bloody button pushing. It had a strong heroine and an appealingly strange mythology. If the gore this time is too much for you to sleep at night, everything else around it may help.

Leone’s talent for tone control and his ability to shift from...chaotic, blood-soaked joy into a horrifying, blood-soaked hopelessness...makes Terrifier 3 work as more than a special effects exhibition.

A gory third helping for fans with a strong stomach for such a bloody flick.

It's not just that the script matters so little, it's that nothing does—plot, character, sense, et al. are just factors that can always be arbitrarily sacrificed to allow for another viscera-clogged bloodbath.
In its zeal to constantly top itself, much like its predecessor, Terrifier 3 is often a numbing experience.
It is a holiday black mass welcoming the historic arrival of a new cinematic dark age with endless fountains of fake blood and popcorn butter.

Terrifier 3 has no limitations. Art the Clown is still the scariest slasher out there.

Part of what makes Art the Clown compelling is the outstanding performance of David Howard Thornton, whose mime work is superb when portraying the sadistic Pierrot clown.

Art the Clown continues to climb towards the upper tier of horror movie baddies and Lauren LaVera has earned her spot as a legitimate scream queen. And all under the guidance of Damien Leone who looks to have a bonafide hit on his hands.

Terrifier 3 looks to cement Art (David Howard Thornton) and director Damien Leone in the horror Hall of Fame. While the effects are god-tier, the story misses the mark in nearly every way.

continues to confront us with the ever-uncomfortable question of not just what we are willing to watch, but why. And there is more to come. A cliffhanger ending suggests that this third entry is no trilogy closer. Art, you see, good or bad, never dies.

The film proffers plenty of funny gifts along these lines, foremost among them a written-for-the-film Christmas tune rivaling the Muppet Christmas Carol’s gold standard, but the real reason for the season is the simple, honest lust for carnage.

The film is thus exactly what you'd expect from a slasher sequel starring its predecessor's survivors. [But] the more [Leone] seems to skew away from the cheap vaudeville gags towards [a] sort of sinister hellscape, the more invested I become.

Art the Clown still brings Terrifier 3 to the top of the body heap, reminding audiences that he’s the new slasher movie king.

David Howard Thornton cements himself as an iconic horror villain much like Robert Englund as Freddy Kruger. Thornton disappears behind Art the Clown’s makeup and teeth to be somehow disturbingly funny and equally terrifying.
Axe-splittingly funny in a vicious way and relentlessly grotesque, Damien Leone's Terrifier 3 is a jolly addition to the growing Art the Clown canon.
Nobody is pushing horror boundaries quite like the writer-director Damien Leone.

Damien Leone ups the ante with a bigger budget and some bigger names, but the undeniable attraction of these films is the devilishly puckish mime who amuses himself with gruesome, gory mayhem.

Easily the best of the franchise & destined to be a Holiday Classic for Horror fans to watch! Brutal, gnarly, gritty, & insanely badass! Art has never been more gleeful & creative! The progression Sienna is brilliant But Victoria might steal the show!

A film that's almost a guilty pleasure. I don't think it's the most groundbreaking thing, but I think it's entertainment, and smart entertainment.

Terrifier 3 offers more of what you’ve come to love or hate from the franchise while also diving into what makes these characters tick. The Terrifier films are generally horror that honk in blood-soaked happiness.

Terrifier 3 is a visceral thrill ride that delivers on its promise of brutal gore and chaotic mayhem. While the story feels a bit obligatory in linking the Christmas-themed carnage, it manages to inject a dose of dark humor that keeps things entertaining.

Terrifier 3 is decking the halls with a triumphant celebration that’s horrifying for all the right reasons and snaps into focus what it is that Leone does singularly well. That may or may not win people over, but it shouldn’t lose any repeat customers.

Terrifier 3 gives fans exactly what they want—more memorable kills than ever. It's a darker, meaner film, which some may find less playful than the last. However, the Christmas setting adds a fresh and lively twist to the brutality.
